paper_a.title: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer

paper_b.arxiv_id: Bernstein-Vazirani 1997 (registry mismatch: paper318 is actually Bernstein-Vazirani 'Quantum complexity theory' SIAM J. Comput., not Simon 1994)
paper_b.title: Quantum complexity theory

metadata.description: Shor's paper (paper_a) extends the quantum-algorithmic Fourier-sampling framework that Bernstein-Vazirani (paper_b) develop to factoring and discrete logarithm. Paper_b builds the QTM model, the universal QTM, the BQP definition, the Hadamard/Fourier-sampling primitive, and proves its 'recursive Fourier sampling' oracle separation; paper_a uses essentially the same QFT-based interference idea with a non-binary modulus q to extract periods from group elements. The papers are therefore in an EXT relationship: paper_a applies and generalises paper_b's Fourier-sampling technique (with QFT mod q replacing the Hadamard $\bmod 2$ transform). Note: paper318 is Bernstein-Vazirani, not Simon as the pair name suggests; alignment is performed on actual contents.

matches.explanation: Both define BQP. Shor describes BQP as 'functions computable in polynomial time on a quantum computer with bounded error probability; the quantum analogue of BPP'. Bernstein-Vazirani give the foundational definition: class accepted with probability >=2/3 by polynomial-time QTMs. Same complexity class, paper_b being its definitional source which Shor implicitly cites.

Both papers set up the underlying quantum computing model. Shor uses the gate-array (quantum circuit) formulation: quantum state superposition (DP317.2), local unitary transformations (DP317.3), gate arrays (DP317.1). Bernstein-Vazirani use the Quantum Turing Machine formulation: QTM (DP318.1), well-formed QTM (DP318.2 -- unitary evolution), and measurement (DP318.3). Both formalisms are computationally equivalent (BV prove this in Section 7) but use different basic objects, so analogous rather than exact.

Shor's quantum Fourier transform $A_q: |a\rangle \mapsto q^{-1/2}\sum_c \exp(2\pi i ac/q)|c\rangle$ over $\mathbb{Z}_q$ (with $q = 2^l$) is the natural extension of Bernstein-Vazirani's Hadamard transform $H_n$ on $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ (TP318.14) and its associated DFT identity (EP318.3) over $\{-1,+1\}$. Both are unitary character-sum transforms; Shor's is the cyclic-group QFT that generalises BV's $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ Hadamard. Analogous rather than exact because the modulus differs (general $q$ vs $2^n$).

Coppersmith's QFT circuit construction (AP317.2: $l(l-1)/2$ gates for $q=2^l$ using $R_j$ and $S_{j,k}$, plus the gate sequence in EP317.2) is the modulus-$2^l$ counterpart of BV's Hadamard transform QTM (TP318.14: $H_n$ in $2n+4$ steps). For $q=2^l$ the QFT factors via the Hadamard plus controlled-phase corrections; in the simple case $q$ a power of two, applying just the Hadamards (no $S_{j,k}$) is exactly BV's construction. Analogous: Shor's circuit is the strict generalisation.

Both algorithms have the same five-step Fourier-sampling structure. BV's Fourier sampling QTM (AP318.5): (1) Hadamard on $0^n$, (2) compute $f$, (3) phase by $f(i)$, (4) reverse step 2, (5) Hadamard, then measure. Shor's order-finding (AP317.3): (1) prepare uniform superposition (Hadamards on $|0\rangle$), (2) compute $x^a \bmod n$ in second register, (3) [interference is automatic from the second-register entanglement], (4) [no explicit reverse], (5) apply QFT $A_q$, then measure. Same template (Hadamard-compute-QFT-measure); Shor uses entanglement instead of phase kickback and QFT mod $q$ instead of Hadamard. Analogous rather than exact.

Order-finding mod $n$ (ProbP317.2 + AP317.3) is the period-finding instance of the general Fourier-sampling problem (DP318.19 + TP318.15 + AP318.5). BV's Fourier sampling samples $s$ with probability $|\hat f(s)|^2$ for an arbitrary polynomial-time-computable sign function $g$; Shor's order-finding samples $c$ with probability concentrated on multiples of $q/r$ for the periodic function $a \mapsto x^a \bmod n$. Order finding is the period-detection special case of Fourier sampling over $\mathbb{Z}_q$ rather than $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$. Strong methodological parallel; classification analogous (same template, different domain).

Both papers cite/use the Bennett reversible-simulation theorem. Shor's TP317.2 (Reversible simulation of classical computation) and AP317.7 (Bennett's reversibility transformation) are the same content as BV's reversible-TM development: TP318.3 (Synchronization Theorem), TP318.4 (reversible TMs are well-formed QTMs), TP318.21 (reversible simulation of oblivious deterministic TMs), TP318.22 (reversible computation of one-to-one functions), and DP318.11 (reversible Turing machine). BV provide the rigorous detailed construction; Shor cites it as a black box. Same theorem; exact (the underlying mathematical fact is identical).

Shor's TP317.1 (Universality of two-bit gates: any unitary decomposes into one-bit gates and CNOTs) and BV's unitary decomposition results (TP318.6 / TP318.7 / AP318.1 / AP318.2: any $d\times d$ unitary is approximable by a polynomial-length product of near-trivial matrices, carried out by a fixed QTM) play the same role: both establish that arbitrary unitaries can be assembled from a small fixed gate set. They differ in basis (CNOT+1-bit gates vs near-trivial phase/rotation matrices) and in framework (gate arrays vs QTM), so analogous.

Shor cites Toffoli (DP317.5) and Fredkin (DP317.6) gates as universal sets for reversible classical computation. BV's reversible Turing machine (DP318.11) is the TM-level counterpart: a deterministic TM each of whose configurations has at most one predecessor. Same notion of reversible computation in different machine models (gate-level vs Turing-machine-level). Analogous.

AP317.4 is Shor's quantum factoring algorithm; TP318.24 is BV's external citation of exactly that result ('Shor's factoring/discrete-log algorithm: there exist polynomial-time quantum algorithms for the integer factoring and discrete logarithm problems'). Paper-origin contribution of A is cited verbatim as prior work in B. Origin-aware: paper-origin in A vs external-origin in B is a strong EXT signal.

AP317.5 (Shor's quantum discrete logarithm algorithm) is the discrete-log half of TP318.24, BV's external citation of Shor 1994. Same paper-origin/external pattern as AP317.4; the same external item in B covers both A-side contributions.
TP317.8 is Shor's main theorem (polynomial-time quantum factoring); TP318.24 cites this exact result. Paper-origin contribution of A appears as external citation in B.
TP317.9 is the polynomial-time quantum discrete log result; TP318.24 covers it (and TP317.8) as the same external citation.

Shor's BQP (DP317.4) is positioned via its analogy to BPP. BV give the structural inclusions situating BQP: BPP $\subseteq$ BQP (TP318.10), BQP $\subseteq$ PSPACE (TP318.11), and BQP $\subseteq$ P^#P (TP318.13). Shor's definition is the object whose containing structure BV characterise. Analogous since A defines while B characterises.

LP317.1 / EP317.3 / PP317.3 establish that the order-finding observation probability $|\frac{1}{q}\sum_b \exp(2\pi i b\langle rc\rangle_q/q)|^2$ is at least $4/(\pi^2 r^2)$. The corresponding element in BV is the discrete Fourier / Hadamard identity EP318.3 with Parseval $\sum_x |f(x)|^2 = \sum_s |\hat f(s)|^2$. Both extract probability mass from a Fourier transform of a periodic signal, but Shor's bound is for $\mathbb{Z}_q$ with imperfect alignment ($q$ not a multiple of $r$) while BV's is the clean Parseval over $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$. Analogous.

Shor's remark RP317.2 ('the order-finding algorithm works for any permutation $f$ on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ whose iterates are computable in poly($\log n, \log k$)') is a direct gesture toward the general Fourier-sampling viewpoint formalised by BV in DP318.19 and TP318.15: any polynomial-time computable function can be Fourier-sampled. Analogous: Shor states the generalisation informally, BV develop it as the foundational primitive.

Shor's main quantum subroutines (order finding AP317.3, factoring AP317.4, discrete log AP317.5) all rely on a single QFT round to extract periodicity. BV's recursive Fourier sampling (AP318.6) is structurally similar (Hadamard, compute, phase, reverse, Hadamard, query) but recursed across a tree to give the strongest known oracle separation. Both are 'Fourier-sampling-based' quantum algorithms but solve different problems and have different recursive structure. Low-confidence analogy: methodological family relationship.

Reversible modular exponentiation (AP317.1) is a Shor-specific subroutine (computes $x^a \bmod n$ reversibly with $O(l^3)$ gates). BV's paper develops generic reversible TM machinery but has no number-theoretic counterpart.
Modular exponentiation problem (DP317.7) is a number-theoretic primitive specific to Shor's algorithm; no corresponding object in BV.
Order of an element mod $n$ (DP317.9) is number-theoretic; not present in BV.
Discrete logarithm (DP317.10) is number-theoretic; not present in BV.
Integer factorization problem (ProbP317.1) is the target of Shor's paper; BV do not address this concrete problem.
Discrete logarithm problem (ProbP317.3); not addressed in BV.
Correctness of quantum order-finding (TP317.7) is a Shor-specific result with no BV analogue.

Continued-fraction recovery of $d/r$ (LP317.2) and the associated Diophantine condition $|c/q-d/r|\le 1/(2q)$ (EP317.4) are post-processing steps tailored to extracting integer periods from Fourier samples mod $q$; no analogous classical post-processing appears in BV's Fourier-sampling framework.
Discrete-log specific lemmas (probability of good output LP317.3, count of good $(c,d)$ pairs LP317.4, recovering $r$ from samples LP317.5) have no counterpart in BV.

Shor's L1 proofs are specific to factoring/order-finding/discrete-log correctness; BV's proofs serve QTM model construction, universality, and oracle separation. No L1 proof-level correspondence beyond the loose Fourier-sampling parallel already captured in the LP317.1 <-> EP318.3 match.

BV-specific QTM-machinery definitions (simulation with slowdown, $\epsilon$-close QTMs, halting, well-behaved/stationary, normal form, unidirectional, multi-track, restricted updates, partial QTM, $\epsilon$-close to unitary, near-trivial unitary) are foundational model-theoretic objects that have no counterpart in Shor's circuit-model paper.
QTM carrying out a transformation (DP318.16) is internal BV machinery; Shor takes the gate-array model as primitive and does not need this formalism.
Oracle QTM (DP318.17) is BV-specific; Shor's paper does not use oracles.
Recursive Fourier sampling / language $R^O$ (DP318.20) and hit / fixed-by-constraint / run (DP318.21) are BV's oracle-separation contributions; no Shor counterpart.
Efficiently computable amplitudes $\tilde{\mathbb{C}}$ (AssumP318.1) is a model assumption specific to BV's QTM; Shor implicitly assumes a similar discreteness but does not formalise it.
Variation-distance and error-accumulation lemmas (LP318.1, TP318.1, TP318.2, CP318.1) are precision-analysis machinery for the universal QTM; Shor does not analyse precision at this level.

BV's library of QTM-construction lemmas (passive track, track permutation, swap-transitions, union, state insertion, dovetailing, branching, reversal, looping, change of basis, interleaving, unidirection, completion) are internal to building the universal QTM. Shor uses the gate model and needs none of this.
Local conditions for QTM well-formedness (TP318.5: unit length / orthogonality / separability) is a QTM-specific characterisation with no counterpart in Shor's circuit model.
Norm bounds and approximation lemmas for unitary decomposition (LP318.15-19) are technical lemmas supporting BV's universal-QTM construction; not in Shor.

BV's efficient universal QTM (TP318.8) and its STEP/full procedures (AP318.3, AP318.4) are the central paper-origin contribution of B. Shor takes universality as given (his TP317.1 cites a different universality result for circuits) and does not produce a universal machine.
P $\subseteq$ EQP (TP318.9) is a structural inclusion specific to BV; Shor does not state structural complexity inclusions.
Clean BQP machine / amplification (TP318.12) is BV-internal; not in Shor.
Reversal of an oracle QTM (LP318.20) is oracle machinery; not in Shor.
Recursive Fourier sampling oracle results (TP318.16, LP318.21, TP318.17, CP318.2) constitute BV's main oracle-separation contribution; Shor's paper has no oracle-separation content.
QTM well-formed iff unitary (TP318.18) is QTM-internal; Shor's circuit model is unitary by construction.

Reversibility characterisation, generalised reversible TM simulation, predecessor-uniqueness corollary, completion of partial reversible $\delta$, and reversible string-exchange/copy machines are all BV's reversible-TM machinery (Appendix B). Shor uses the high-level reversibility theorem (TP317.2 / AP317.7) but none of these explicit constructions.
